rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Analysis and interpretation  ·  Analysis names what is on the page: diction, image, structure, and speaker. Interpretation says what those choices do for meaning. Keep the two moves separate so a reading stays tied to the text.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Analysis ladder: device → effect → theme — never stop at naming a device; the marks are in what it ACHIEVES and what it MEANS.  ·  Trick 2: Every interpretation must be text-anchored: claim + quotation + explanation; a claim without quotation sits in the lower band.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. A close-reading order  ·  Start with the title and the speaker. Mark one striking word or image, then describe the form: line length, repetition, or a shift in tone. Only after that, state a meaning and quote the line that supports it.  ·  ### 3. Theme and tone

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Trick 3: Title, opening line and ending carry authorial intent — analyse all three when asked about the writer's purpose.  ·  define + example each sub-idea: literary analysis, interpretation.  ·  one worked example for "Literary Analysis and Interpretation" — check units / edge cases.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: recall card: definition → formula → limit → one error to avoid.  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.  ·  Theme is the idea the text keeps returning to. Tone is the speaker's attitude toward the subject. A theme such as loss needs a tone such as bitter or resigned, each backed by a phrase from the text.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ### 4. Choosing between readings  ·  Two interpretations can both be possible. Prefer the one that accounts for more of the text and does not ignore a clear contradiction. Say which lines the weaker reading leaves out.  ·  ### 5. A short example

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A story that ends with an open door: analysis records the image. Interpretation might call it freedom or unfinished danger.
